items.title: Rocket posts $709M profit in Q3 despite tougher mortgage market
items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. In September, Rocket Mortgage adopted VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for eligible loans. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. Outlook for Q4 2026 Rocket expects adjusted revenue of $2.1 billion to $2.3 billion in Q4, below the $2.5 billion to $2.7 billion range it projected for Q3 in its previous earnings report. Brown said that the company expects the market to weaken further as mortgage rates remain elevated and seasonal trends reduce activity. The company estimated purchase mortgage applications were down nearly 20% year over year, while refinance applications had fallen more than 50%. items.title: Dan Wagner To Head Lee & Associates In Atlanta: The Atlanta Deal Sheet
items.description: Lee & Associates in Atlanta is elevating its chief data officer to lead the office after current CEO Dave Howard steps down. Courtesy of Lee & Associates Lee & Associates Atlanta's Dan Wagner Lee & Associates Chief Data Officer Dan Wagner has been named president and CEO of the Atlanta office, effective Jan. 1, replacing Howard, who has led the Atlanta office since 2020, the company announced this week. Howard will continue in a consulting role with Lee & Associates, assisting other area offices in the U.S. with their growth plans, the company said. During his six-year tenure in Atlanta, Howard expanded the brokerage office by 60%, including adding a medical office team, and positioned the Atlanta office among the top five Lee & Associates offices in the U.S. “I was brought to Atlanta to grow this company, and I’m proud of what our team has accomplished,” Howard said in the release. “Dan is the right person to lead the next chapter, and I look forward to supporting the firm and helping our people continue to grow.” A former senior research leader at CBRE, Wagner joined Lee & Associates in 2022 and assisted in growing its junior associate program, which fostered leaders within the brokerage firm. Wagner has more than 30 years of CRE experience. PERSONNEL Chicago-based Kiser Group announced that it is opening an Atlanta office for its multifamily investment sales platform and tapped Tyler Arnold as an adviser for the region. Arnold is Kiser’s first Atlanta broker, focused on apartment sales throughout Metro Atlanta. Prior to Kiser, Arnold served as a land specialist at PureLand Real Estate and was formerly a project engineer at the Community Construction Group. “Our expansion into Atlanta reflects both opportunity and intention,” Kiser Chief Revenue Officer Mike Mosher said in a press release. “We wanted someone who understands the market and the mechanics of multifamily ownership, and Tyler brings that full picture.” *** A shift in Atlanta’s CRE industry is introducing two new leaders, one at a prominent industry association and the other at a fast-growing brokerage firm. The Atlanta Commercial Board of Realtors named Haley Casola as its executive director, succeeding Robin Godwin, who is leaving the board after nine years. Casola, who was hired in June, is part of a succession plan “years in the making,” the ACBR said in a press release. Casola most recently was a project manager with the Georgia Department of Economic Development. Godwin was named chief operating officer of Partners Real Estate's southeast region. She will be working closely with Managing Partner John O’Neill to support Partners' expansion across the region, the Atlanta Business Chronicle reported . Godwin is tasked with overseeing finance and accounting coordination, human resources, brokerage and community support and integrating new offices and teams, according to the ABC. She takes the helm in January. SALES Google Maps Wellstar Health System purchased its Marietta hospital campus at 340 Kennestone Hospital Blvd. on Oct. 22 for $33.4M from Healthcare Realty Trust, according to sales tax records in the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database. Wellstar spokesperson Matt O’Connor confirmed the transaction to Bisnow in an email. “We’ve been a tenant in that building. We just had the opportunity to purchase it,” he said. *** RCG Ventures purchased Tucker Meridian Shopping Center, a 208K SF retail center at 4310 LaVista Road, from Ben F. Kushner Co. for an undisclosed sum, according to a Colliers press release. No records reflected the price as of the time of publication. The center, built in 2017 and anchored by Sprouts Farmers Market, Dick’s Sporting Goods, Hobby Lobby, Ross Dress for Less and DSW, was 98% leased at the time of the sale. Colliers’ Henry Kushner and Joe Montgomery sold the property. Ben F. Kushner obtained a $28.7M loan last year from Seacoast National Bank that was set to mature in July 2029, according to the Georgia Superior Court Clerks' Cooperative Authority database. items.title: RXR Marketing Executive Lauren Maturo Dies At 32
items.description: Lauren Maturo, a vice president of marketing at New York City real estate giant RXR, died Saturday night at the age of 32. Courtesy of RXR Lauren Maturo, vice president of marketing at RXR, died Saturday. Maturo was killed in a multivehicle crash on the Garden State Parkway in Toms River, New Jersey, caused by a tractor-trailer stopping behind a disabled car, News12 New Jersey first reported . RXR Chairman and CEO Scott Rechler announced Maturo's death in a LinkedIn post Wednesday . “Lauren Maturo was a bright light who made every room she entered feel a little warmer,” Rechler's post says. “She was a treasured member of the RXR team and a dear friend to so many of us.” Maturo lived in Syosset, New York, Commercial Observer reported . She is survived by her parents, Paula Maturo and Michael Maturo, who is RXR's president, as well as sisters Elise Maturo and Jillian Maturo. A wake was held Thursday afternoon, and her funeral Mass is planned for Friday morning . Her family has asked attendees to wear bright colors as a tribute, Rechler said in his LinkedIn post. “Our industry has lost an exceptional talent,” Sarah Berman , president of marketing firm The Berman Group, told Bisnow by email from her train on the way to Maturo’s wake. “Those who knew Lauren have lost something far greater: a vibrant, generous spirit whose creativity, kindness and passion made everything and everyone around her brighter.” Lauren Maturo spent eight years building a marketing career and had made it her mission to mentor younger associates at the development firm, Commercial Observer reported. In that time, she worked with creative studio SDX Studio on properties in RXR’s portfolio, including the Starrett-Lehigh Building and Pier 57 . Lauren Maturo was also in her second year of pursuing a master's degree in real estate from New York University’s Schack Institute of Real Estate and would have graduated next December, according to her LinkedIn page. She was an athlete from an early age. According to Commercial Observer, Lauren Maturo played basketball for Syosset High School and later played basketball and track and field at Carnegie Mellon University. She was also involved in the 9/11 Memorial & Museum’s annual charity run, Jan Llanes, vice president of corporate giving at the museum, told Commercial Observer. Tributes to Lauren Maturo on an obituary page describe her as a warm, thoughtful community member who championed those around her. “Lauren inspired me,” Yelle Belle, a marketing executive at RXR, wrote in a post on Maturo’s obituary page. “She showed me what it looked like to authentically be yourself at work.” Related Topics: New York University Schack Institute of Real Estate , Pier 57 , RXR Realty , Starrett-Lehigh

items.title: GGP To Redevelop Former Dick's Sporting Goods Store At Frisco's Stonebriar Centre
items.description: The Frisco mall is planning a radical reimagining of an anchor space that was recently vacated. Courtesy of GGP A rendering of the planned redevelopment of a former Dick's Sporting Goods at Stonebriar Centre in Frisco Stonebriar Centre owner GGP will redevelop the former Dick’s Sporting Goods space on the mall’s north side into a covered outdoor area surrounded by restaurants and retailers. The company, which is Brookfield 's retail division, didn’t disclose the cost of the planned redevelopment or any tenants but said the project would bring new energy and fresh opportunities to the mall. “Our redevelopment plans represent a new era for this beloved shopping center, and we look forward to sharing details about what’s ahead as this exciting transformation takes shape,” GGP Head of Development Adam Tritt said in a statement sent to Bisnow . Work on the redevelopment, which appears to be similar to The District at Willow Bend area of Plano's The Shops at Willow Bend mall, is expected to begin in the first quarter of 2027, The Dallas Morning News reported . The District at Willow Bend features restaurants such as Knife Steakhouse, Whistle Britches and Mexican Bar Co. around an outdoor courtyard just outside the Plano mall. A rendering of the Stonebriar Centre project shows an outdoor covered area leading to a mall entrance with restaurant patios on either side of the space. Dick’s Sporting Goods vacated the space to open a new concept in the mall’s former Sears space. Its House of Sport store will offer interactive activities such as golf simulators, putting greens and rock-climbing walls in addition to the chain's regular athletic gear and apparel. Dick's House of Sport is slated to open Nov. 13. Stonebriar Centre is one of the strongest-performing malls in GGP's portfolio, Vice President of Leasing Randy Holcombe told Bisnow last month. The 1.7M SF mall's visitor totals have risen every year since the pandemic and were up nearly 3% through the first eight months of the year, according to data from Placer.ai . GGP has catered its tenant mix to the city’s affluent, well-educated customers, with Holcombe noting that Stonebriar has opened more than 90K SF of new stores over the past few years. items.title: From Pandemic Darling To Cautionary Tale: Pickleball Clubs Face A Reckoning After Betting Big On Retail Space
items.description: Pickleball ’s post-pandemic popularity prompted retail purveyors across the country to create concepts in malls and former big-box stores to attract players, but some of their real estate deals have turned sour as markets have become saturated with court options. After years as the fastest-growing sport in the U.S. , pickleball court construction has slowed despite participation figures rising nearly 23% last year. Facility franchisor The Picklr ’s Oct. 9 bankruptcy filing underscores the risks of aggressive expansion in the increasingly competitive market. “As people were catching the pickleball bug, they were a little bit pie-in-the-sky about how their business models could look, and they accepted real estate deals that they probably shouldn't have because they were overly bullish,” said Ross Chaifetz, managing director at private investment firm Chaifetz Group. Unsplash/Hoi Pham The expansion of public pickleball courts across the 100 biggest U.S. cities has slowed significantly , dropping from 14% growth in 2024 to just 4% in 2026, Axios reported. Indoor expansions have similarly cooled off as retailers become more selective with their growth plans, according to pickleball media site The Dink . However, the Sports & Fitness Industry Association's 2026 Single Sport Report showed that pickleball participation rose from nearly 20 million players in 2024 to more than 24 million last year. Chaifetz believes that presents a best-case scenario for the remaining pickleball businesses to prosper. "You have an increasing amount of demand and an increasing player pool that will now be redirected to a smaller supply count of facilities and places to play," Chaifetz said. The pickleball boom prompted mall operators to lean into the trend as a demand driver throughout 2023 to help fill vacant store space. But the wave of attention for the sport had crested by late 2024, according to FanEquity , a platform that tracks cultural relevance and fan behavior similarly to how financial market analysts watch stocks. Still, The Picklr and five other prominent pickleball brands continued expanding through the first nine months of 2026, opening more than 50 new clubs during that time, according to The Dink. Now, the fast build-out in major markets across the country has caught up with the industry. In Northern California, new pickleball leasing activity has slowed due to oversupply in the market, JLL Sacramento Senior Vice President John Brecher said. “The market is in a let-the-dust-settle phase,” Brecher told Bisnow . “Operators, landlords and investors want to see how membership ramps up, where the customer demand actually is and which trade areas are already saturated before they commit to the next round of deals.” The Picklr is the poster child for why operators and landlords alike are hesitant to rush into leases. Founded in 2021, The Picklr began franchising in 2023 and reached a $59M valuation the following year. The company sold over 300 franchises by mid-2024 and had plans for clubs in more than 32 states by early 2025. Bisnow/Nancy Sheppard The Picklr's parent company filed for bankruptcy in early October, though many franchise locations remain open. However, its operating footprint grew more gradually than those early projections, as the company had just 76 franchise locations before filing for bankruptcy. “In a lot of ways, it's somewhat predictable if you look at any high-growth trend or fad … there's always an overshoot,” Chaifetz said. The Picklr did not respond to Bisnow ’s requests for an interview. CEO Jorge Barragan told the Sports Business Journal that the bankruptcy stemmed from The Picklr’s lease guarantees for around 40 early franchisees that became too costly for the company. The Picklr generated $10.3M in revenue last year but still recorded a $4.4M loss, with total liabilities reaching around $19M by the end of the first quarter of this year. The company isn't the only chain that has faced financial difficulties in recent years, as PickleRage and Pickleball Kingdom have also shuttered franchise locations . The economics of small pickleball clubs can prove challenging, as most 10-court facilities have rents of about $30K to $50K per month for spaces of 20K SF to 40K SF, Heleus Holdings CEO West Shaw wrote for The Dink . Clubs with 10 or fewer courts typically pull in around $8K per court every month, according to industry performance data from Johns Design & Consulting . But a $50K rent plus expenses such as payroll, utilities, upkeep, marketing and inventory can total more than $85K per month, meaning clubs need to make more than $1M per year to break even, according to Shaw. Private equity and venture capital flooded the pickleball space before the market understood how to properly monetize demand for the sport, according to Painted Hospitality CEO Justin Amick, whose company operates entertainment-driven concepts with bars and restaurants. While exact figures of pickleball’s U.S. footprint aren’t available, there is likely more than 14.7M SF devoted to the sport at indoor venues, as data analytics company FRANdata reported brands typically need 20K SF to 40K SF and The Club Scout lists 735 indoor clubs . The retail sector is well positioned to absorb pickleball club closures, as the sector’s third-quarter national vacancy rate was 4.3% , which Colliers noted was near historic lows. While Northern California hasn’t seen any pickleball closures as of late, Brecher said junior anchor space in well-located trade areas remains in demand with a variety of tenants. Cities like Austin, Seattle and New York have become major pickleball hubs as the sport has grown. But The Picklr's bankruptcy will make investors nationwide think twice before signing on to future pickleball-related projects, Custom Capital CEO Jason Milton said. “Some of these indoor pickleball court clubs charge $40-$50 a month,” Milton told Bisnow . “If you're in a sunny area and you can play outside, that's free.” Many p

items.title: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q
items.description: Pennymac sees more layoffs as originations plummet in 3Q By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 7:27 p.m. EDT | Updated October 29, 2026, 8:21 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Pennymac posted its lowest mortgage origination and acquisition volume since the first quarter of 2024. Supporting Data: While the company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, its servicing pretax income rose to $99 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. PennyMac Financial Services is making deeper cost cuts after its originations fell 30% this summer. The lender and servicer will slash $160 million in annualized operating expenses in the coming months as it anticipates higher-for-longer rates, it said Thursday. That expands on cuts that began this summer in response to some of the worst mortgage market conditions this decade. Processing Content While the company remained well in the black for the third quarter, its combined origination segment volume of $24.4 billion was its lowest mark since the first quarter of 2024. Chairman and CEO David Spector, in an earnings call Thursday evening, described the current landscape as "one of the most constrained origination environments our industry has seen since 2023." Pennymac didn't provide additional details about staff reductions . For the third quarter, Pennymac posted a $29 million profit, surpassing the $22 million net income in the second quarter. That was still a fraction of the $181.5 million profit Pennymac posted at the same time last year. Although elevated rates and heightened competition battered origination performance, the company highlighted stronger income in servicing, and green shoots in artificial intelligence advancements. Inside the numbers The company posted a $7 million loss in production segment pretax income, after marks of $38 million and $122.9 million in the prior quarter and year-ago periods, respectively. Servicing pretax income meanwhile rose to $99 million, soaring from $22 million in the second quarter but falling from $157 million a year ago. Pennymac also agreed to sell $29 billion in unpaid principal balance of low-rate conventional mortgage servicing rights, it said. It plans to redeploy the $490 million in proceeds to reduce higher-cost debt, and repurchase common shares. The servicing book ended the quarter slightly up around $737 billion. Revenues fell to end the period at $469 million, declines of 6% quarterly and 26% annually. Executive outlook Company leaders expanded on origination trends, with Pennymac posting greater consumer direct margins with more closed-end second lien volume. Spector also suggested competitive pressures from the government-sponsored enterprises' cash window for smaller brokerages, and the industry leaders' aggressive pricing. "We're picking and choosing our spots, and maintaining market share, and not really getting too caught up in market share at levels that are just not sustainable or that one can rationalize," said Spector. Pennymac also touted its AI advancements, noting that its tech spending is coming down. The lender has 22 proprietary AI agents live in production and is developing 17 more, while its proprietary AI voice agent supported over 1,600 rate locks in the third quarter. "This will allow us to maintain lean operation in today's constrained environment, while ensuring substantial operating leverage when origination volumes normalize," Spector said of the company's AI prowess. What's ahead The firm also announced some executive moves, as President and Chief Mortgage Banking Officer Doug Jones will retire next June. Chief Strategy Officer Kevin Ryan will be elevated to chief financial officer in January, while current CFO Daniel Perotti will remain in that role through the end of the year. Pennymac's Cenlar deal, which will bring its servicing book past $1 trillion , is now expected to close early next year, as executives said they're waiting on one remaining state approval. Processing Content Rocket marked four financial quarters of owning Mr. Cooper with its highest profit margins in five years, at a time when mortgage rates reached their highest levels since 2003. The quarter results were very good, both in terms of profit and production. But going forward, the mortgage environment will be tough, not just in the fourth quarter, but also throughout 2027, Rocket executives said on the earnings call. They were even more bearish than industry forecasts from the Mortgage Bankers Association and Fannie Mae. The fourth quarter normally is a low one production-wise for the industry and this one is being impacted at a time when mortgage rates are at levels not seen in two decades, said Brian Brown, Rocket Cos. president and chief financial officer. "We've been calling for a smaller market than the industry forecast, and that's pretty much exactly what we've seen quarter after quarter after quarter," Krishna said. "When you look at 2027, you know the forecasts are below $2 trillion; we think it could actually be even smaller still." In this environment, the executives pointed out that Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance. What was Rocket's third quarter volume? In the wholesale channel, "over 200 brokers have now activated with Rocket, that represents almost $12 billion in potential annualized volume," Krishna said. "So, four consecutive quarters of expanding margins, taking share and better economics. That's kind of the combination that we're solving for." In the current period, Brown said per channel margins are running similar to the third quarter. The company ended the quarter with a $2 trillion mortgage servicing portfolio. Rocket's MSR sales during the period totaled $23 billion, generating $379 million of cash proceeds. Furthermore, management noted it retained subservicing and recapture rights on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Rocket reports a GAAP profit The third quarter was the second consecutive quarter of GAAP profitability for Rocket, with net income of $709 million. This compared with net income of $34 million in the second quarter, and a loss of $124 million one year ago. When asked about competition, Krishna responded "I think the reality is the market is literally testing every single lender, and that's like a good news, bad news story. I think the good news is if you have a strong business model, guess what? It's going to shine through. But the bad news is if you have a flaw in your business model, it's going to get exposed." Earlier Brown noted in the past lenders have used pricing as a lever to drive volume in times of scarce originations. He is not seeing as much of it right now. items.title: Enterprise Bank & Trust exits mortgage industry, cites scale
items.description: Enterprise Bank & Trust exits mortgage industry, cites scale By Colin McNamara Published October 29, 2026, 5:59 p.m. EDT 2 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Why depository banks continue to exit the mortgage industry. What's at Stake: Local homebuyers seeking mortgage options as more regional depositories exit the origination space. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Another depository is exiting the mortgage industry in order to cut expenses, continuing a trend that has persisted through the current high-rate environment . Processing Content Enterprise Bank & Trust, headquartered in Clayton, Missouri, confirmed the move on its third-quarter earnings call last week, saying it looked at multiple areas of business in the company that were subscale. "We also recently announced that we're exiting the mortgage business as it relates to an originator," said Jim Lally, CEO of Enterprise Financial Services Corp., on the call. "So we're taking expenses out where we're not adding a great deal of value and really can scale." Jim Lally, CEO of Enterprise Financial Services Corp. Enterprise joins Michigan-based Northpointe Bank as depositories to leave the mortgage space in October. Northpointe announced it sold its distributed retail and consumer direct channels to CMG Financial , an independent mortgage bank. Northpointe Chairman and CEO Chuck Williams said in an earnings call last week that volumes could no longer carry the overhead of mortgage operations, citing economic headwinds. Another executive said the deal doesn't involve the transfer of loans and similar assets. The bank will retain other lending activity, including a mortgage purchase program comparable to warehouse lending. Under the terms of the agreement, CMG will pay Northpointe 15 basis points on any first-lien mortgage originations closed through the mortgage origination channels until Dec. 31, 2028, the bank announced in a press release this week. Unlike the Northpointe transaction, Enterprise has not announced a buyer or referral partner for its mortgage business. Why banks should stay in mortgage Despite recent examples, Rich Swerbinsky, executive director of the Ohio Mortgage Bankers Association and founder of Upward & Onward Consulting, said banks that previously left the mortgage industry, or never conducted business in it, have been rethinking their decision. At the American Bankers Association's annual conference, multiple banking executives made the case for staying in mortgage without building a 40-person department, Swerbinsky said. "I think the wind's at the back of depositories right now," he wrote in his newsletter, Swerbs Blurbs, Wednesday. "Capital rules are loosening, portfolio lending is back in play, talent is moving, and all this AI has people craving local, in-person relationships. Consumers need more options, especially local ones." Enterprise's third-quarter results In addition to shutting down its mortgage business, the company withdrew from some banking activities in markets, particularly in the West, where it lacked interest to properly compete, Lally said in the call. The moves come after Enterprise posted continued growth in its broader lending business. The company recorded a 3.8% quarterly and 6.6% annual increase in total loans to $12.3 billion but a net income of $42.4 million, which was down 6.2% year over year. items.description: New York & Tri-State CRE News In Your Inbox. Sign up for Connect emails to stay informed with CRE stories that are 150 words or less. New York & Tri-State + Finance | October 29, 2026 By: Paul Bubny New York People and Company News, Week of Oct. 30, 2026 SL Green Realty Corp. announced that Jason Maurer has joined the company as managing director, overseeing retail leasing across the company’s portfolio and office leasing for Green Property Services, SL Green’s growing third-party asset management platform. Maurer joins SL Green from Brookfield Properties, where he most recently served as EVP and Head of Leasing for North America. JLL has appointed Angela Gentry as Market Lead for New York, where she will lead growth strategy, financial performance, recruitment and talent development alongside Peter Riguardi, Chairman and President of the New York Tri-State Region. Since joining JLL in 2022, Gentry has helped develop and scale the firm’s business development platform, supporting more than $230 million in business pursuits and contributing to a 131% increase in new business opportunities. She most recently served as Vice Chairman, Leasing Advisory. King & Spalding announced that Eddie Frastai has joined the firm as a partner in its Real Estate & Funds practice group. He is based in the New York office and joins King & Spalding from Clifford Chance, where he was a partner. Experienced life sciences and pharmaceutical manufacturing industry leader Al Martino recently joined the Consigli Construction Co., Inc. team as Regional Director – NJ/PA. Equipped with more than 25 years of wide-ranging ownership expertise in the delivery, engineering and asset management of complex facilities and programs for global clients, Martino will lead Consigli's regional operations and business development efforts. Anne S. Babineau, Shareholder and Senior Counsel – Special Projects in the Real Estate and Redevelopment group at Wilentz, Goldman & Spitzer, P.A., will be inducted into the New Jersey Commercial Real Estate Development Association (CREDA NJ) Hall of Fame at the organization's 2026 President's Awards and Hall of Fame Ceremony on Nov. 2, 2026. CREDA NJ uses these awards to acknowledge the vital roles the recipients play in supporting the industry through their exemplary service and commitment to the chapter. Workplace experience and facility management firm ISS North America and its corporate food service brand Guckenheimer have launched a Hospitality Advisory Board. The new Board was created to define, test and scale the next generation of workplace hospitality across the Americas. Functioning as an active engine to define modern workplace hospitality, the Hospitality Advisory Board will be chaired by Amelia Ekus , who has spent significant time in the restaurant and hospitality space and was recently elevated to the role of Head of Hospitality & Innovation for ISS and Guckenheimer. Helen Herrick, Principal and Managing Director of MBH Architects’ New York office, was honored as one of the five new legionaries inducted into the esteemed Retail Design Legion of Honor during the Retail Design Institute’s 55th International Design Awards program. The ceremony took place on Wednesday, October 21, at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York City. Herrick joins MBH founder John McNulty, inducted in 2023, as the second MBH leader to receive the honor. Rappel will team with Executive Managing Director Andrew Briner, Co-Head, U.S. Capital Markets Kevin Shannon, Vice Chairman Ken White, Associate Director Aaron Banks and Senior Analyst Dillan Argue. In his role, Rappel will focus on institutional industrial investment sales and joint venture equity placement. He brings more than 15 years of commercial real estate experience spanning brokerage, acquisitions, development and asset management. Kidder Mathews has added Mac Hall to the Century City office as a member of The Solomon Healthcare Advisory Team . Hall joins SVP Daniel Solomon and associate VP Jackie Moeller, focusing on the sale of healthcare real estate. Before joining Kidder Mathews, Hall was with Accenture, where he was a client engagement manager specializing in marketing and advertising. Hanley Investment Group Real Estate Advisors has acquired the retail investment sales division of Visintainer Group, combining the two most active retail investment sales firms in California's Central Valley. John Kourafas, CCIM, joins Hanley Investment Group as VP, sales. Jamey Browning joins as transaction manager. Both will remain based in Fresno. Brett Visintainer, CCIM, principal of Visintainer Group, will stay on as a strategic advisor to both teams, focused on clients and 1031 exchange buyers. MVE + Partners , an award-winning architecture and planning firm, has announced 17 promotions, including five new Principals, and the expansion of its downtown Los Angeles office. Promoted to principal are Luis Estrada, Paul Kearney, Raymond Albanesi, Tim Beuchat and Joe McClyde. MVE also announced the following promotions across its architectural, planning and technical teams: Senior Associate Partners: Craig Smith, Hakop Musayelyan, Luisa Ceron and Steven Rosier. Associate Partners: Ana Ramirez, Charbel Moumaji and Martin Torres. Associates: Karen Xiao, Andrea Dinsmore, Jason Jia, Ruben Rivas and Kai Parel-Sewell. The firm is relocating its Los Angeles operations to larger offices at The Bloc, 700 S. Flower St., in downtown's Financial District. Skyline Construction announced the hiring of Steve Dunne as Senior Project Executive. With 39 years of construction industry experience, Dunne is recognized for leading complex projects and campus developments for many of Silicon Valley's most prominent organizations.
